The National Youth Service Corps has warned politicians in Rivers State against offering food, water, drinks or other inducements to corps members who will serve as ad hoc staff of the Independent National Electoral Commission during the 2027 general elections. According to the organization, corps members must be allowed to perform their electoral duties without interference, warning that anyone found accepting inducements from politicians would face appropriate sanctions. The Rivers State Coordinator of the scheme, Moses Oleghe, gave the warning on Thursday while delivering his goodwill message at a state-level stakeholders’ meeting on the 2027 general elections at the INEC headquarters in Port Harcourt. He urged politicians to desist from attempts to influence corps members, insisting that they must maintain their neutrality and integrity throughout the electoral process. Oleghe also appealed to INEC to make adequate provisions for the welfare of corps members, including payment of allowances, transportation and other essential logistics, arguing that providing their entitlements would enable them to cater for their basic needs without depending on politicians. Allow them to do their work. It is a national assignment and they are committed to it. “If INEC pays them their transport, they will not be hungry, so don’t bring food for them. Don’t bring water for them, don’t bring drinks for them. “I can assure this gathering that if all of these are put in place, the corps members are well prepared to deliver on the mandate that they have been given.” The NYSC coordinator, however, raised concerns over the treatment of corps members during previous elections, saying some had been stranded or abandoned by their Supervisory Presiding Officers in unsafe locations, thereby exposing them to danger. He insisted that such experiences would not be tolerated during the 2027 elections, urging INEC to put adequate arrangements in place to protect corps members and ensure their welfare. Oleghe said the NYSC had commenced sensitisation programmes in collaboration with INEC to prepare corps members for their responsibilities during the forthcoming elections. He, however, stressed that the exercise would yield little result without proper planning and coordination among the electoral commission, security agencies and other stakeholders. The NYSC boss urged the Resident Electoral Commissioner to ensure that corps members were trained by personnel with adequate knowledge of the electronic devices and other technologies to be deployed for the elections. He also expressed concern over instances where corps members who had undergone training and reported at Registration Area Centres were replaced during deployment. He said corps members who had made themselves available for training and deployment but were subsequently excluded should be paid their entitlements. Oleghe further called on INEC to improve basic facilities at RAC centres, noting that corps members were often expected to remain at the centres from the afternoon before election day until the conclusion of voting and other electoral activities without adequate provisions. He said facilities such as sleeping mats, drinking water, toilets, soap, tissue paper, electricity and security should be provided at the centres. The coordinator also called for the early release of complete election materials, insisting that no corps member should leave a RAC centre for an assigned polling unit without all the materials required to discharge their duties.
